October 13, 2026




 Guyana Opposition Leader arrested after shooting near senior cop’s home 







GEORGETOWN, Guyana (CMC) – Guyanese police on Tuesday confirmed that they had arrested the country’s Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed and two of his workers following an incident near the home of the head of the Special Branch Unit, Prem Narine.

In the statement, the Guyana Police Force (GPF) said it is investigating an alleged discharge of a loaded firearm with intent and possession of a firearm and ammunition without a licence, following the incident.

The statement said that Narine was at his residence when he reported that he observed a black Toyota Allion motor car bearing registration number PXX 5300 travelling slowly along Barr Street.

“Investigations further revealed that as the vehicle approached his residence on the second occasion, Senior Superintendent Narine heard what appeared to be a gunshot. He took cover and discharged several rounds from his service firearm in the direction of the vehicle, which subsequently drove away,” the police said in the statement.

It said the motor car was later intercepted with three occupants who were later identified as Mohamed, and two of his workers, Mario Mohamed and Eugene Thorne. They were arrested and escorted to the Kitty Police Station.

According to the police statement, a search of the motor car led to the discovery of a .32 Taurus pistol without a serial number, along with three live rounds of .32 ammunition. The three men were subsequently arrested in connection with possession of a firearm and ammunition without a licence.

The police also stated that a .32 spent shell was recovered opposite Narine’s residence while four 9mm spent shells were also recovered.

The firearm, ammunition and spent shells were lodged pending ballistic examination, while CCTV footage from the area will be reviewed as part of the investigation, according to the police statement.

But in a live video broadcast that was being carried out by Mohamed’s sister on social media, the Opposition Leader repeatedly stated that there was an attempt on his life by Narine, who he said fired gunshots repeatedly at the car he was in.

Mohamed reportedly claims that he and his workers were in the area to document what they regard as an abuse of state resources with a large police presence outside the home of the head of the Special Branch.

Mohamed also claimed in the broadcast that the weapon found by the police in the car was planted.

Mohamed and his lawyer, Siand Dhurjon, said the firearm that was located under the accelerator pedal was planted there by police.

The incident on Tuesday occurred several hours before Mohamed is due to appear at the Guyana Court of Appeal for a civil case challenging the constitutionality of several provisions of the Fugitive Offenders Act.

Narine, who has been on the witness stand in the extradition hearing before Chief Magistrate Judy Latchman, has deemed Mohamed a threat to national security and cited his alleged involvement in a number of homicides. He has never been charged with any of those alleged offences.

October 13, 2026




 Teacher shot dead in school in Mexico 







MEXICO CITY, Mexico (AFP)—A teacher was shot dead in a school in the Mexican state of Oaxaca on Tuesday, local prosecutors said.

The incident comes days after a separate attack on another school in northern Mexico, where a school employee died and three more people were wounded.

In Tuesday’s incident, panic erupted among students attending the middle school in the town of San Blas Atempa, local media reported.

Prosecutors said in a statement they have launched an investigation to identify the perpetrators of the attack in which the teacher sustained wounds from the gunfire and later died in hospital.

Earlier this month, two 18-year-old brothers wielded knives during an attack on their former school in the northern city of Torreon, killing a member of staff.

Mexico is overrun by organised crime and drug-related violence, but attacks on schools are rare.

 Police searching for licensed firearm holder accused of shooting spouse in Manchester 







MANCHESTER, Jamaica— Police have launched a manhunt for a licensed firearm holder accused of shooting his wife at their home in Newark near Spur Tree, Manchester, Tuesday morning.

The injured woman, said to be in her 30s, has been admitted at hospital in serious condition.

Residents say about 10:00 am, loud explosions were heard coming from the couple’s home.

“I heard the gunshot and saw a man jump in his car and sped off. The lady called out for help and neighbours took her from under a clothes line and rushed her to hospital. She was pinning out laundry when she was shot,” a resident said.

Detectives processed the scene mid-afternoon Tuesday and said the woman was undergoing surgery up to 4:00 pm.

— Kasey Williams

 WATCH: Protesters hit Duke Street over $40m NaRRA CEO salary, $115m lease plan 







KINGSTON, Jamaica —A group of protesters gathered on Duke Street, downtown Kingston, Tuesday afternoon to register their concerns surrounding several issues, including the recently disclosed $40 million annual salary of the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA), Antony Anderson, and the proposed $115 million to lease Digicel headquarters to house the authority.

The placard-bearing protesters, who were decked out in yellow, questioned the motive surrounding the proposed salary.

“Jamaica does not belong to the prime minister and his members. Jamaica belongs to us. We select you September 3rd. We are telling you need to take directive from us. You don’t lead this country as you feel like you want to lead it.

When you take $50 million to give Major General Antony Anderson, what are you saying to us. $50 million or $40 million just for pay, plus you’re going to pay for the building downtown. I know the agenda that you have; we are telling you this, make it be known for the record: we don’t want Antony Anderson in the building. I am going to tell you this: we are standing up against being in that building downtown,” said Ricardo Hall, a protester.

Another protester, who gave her name as Maroon Queen, called for the resignation of Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang and Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake.

“We’re here to tell Kevin Blake that you’re not doing a good job. You’re acting like it’s a gang, like it’s a criminal organisation. So we need you to step down and we need proper people in the position. That means we’re not talking about being soft on crime. We need someone who loves Jamaica and knows what is happening. Know that there’s corruption in the police force. We already have criminals outside we don’t need criminals inside the police force,” she said.

The group is also raising concerns surrounding the state of the country’s hospitals and slow pace of hurricane relief to affected Jamaicans.

 Central Kingston’s housing stock in dire need of overhaul says MP Williams 







KINGSTON, Jamaica—Member of Parliament (MP) for Kingston Central, Donovan Williams, has acknowledged that “it goes without saying” that the constituency is in need of a massive housing overhaul.

“Much of the housing infrastructure is ageing and is in urgent need of improvement,” Williams said Tuesday in the House of Representatives. The second-term MP was making his contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Constituency Debate.

Williams shared that he has been making some progress in tackling the problem. He told the Parliament that through the New Social Housing Programme and building grants, several multi-family housing solutions have been constructed.

The most recent construction has taken place in the East Palms Housing Development in Kingston Gardens, consisting of eight units which are now complete and scheduled to be handed over this month.

Another 18 units located on Hanover Street in the Tel Aviv community of Parade Gardens are currently under construction.

“Cumulatively to date, we have and will be providing housing solutions to approximately 40 families, and they can all be verified. While we welcome the programme, there are persons independently renovating and improving their housing structures,” said Williams. He lamented that one of the hindrances to housing solutions is the issue of land tenure, the regularisation of land titles being a critical matter.

Williams told the Parliament that a large section of the constituency has already been designated an area under the Registration of Titles, Cadastral Mapping and Tenure Clarification Special Provisions Act, paving the way for systematic land titling.

“We are therefore looking forward to an acceleration of this process in assisting residents with obtaining their titles,” he said while noting that this will have the effect of providing a catalyst for urban renewal and generational wealth creation.

Williams also shared that several properties owned by state agencies have been earmarked for additional social housing developments. He said it was his belief that with a combination of private and government initiatives, there will be ongoing improvements to the housing stock in central Kingston.

-Lynford Simpson

news.title: Trump unlikely to impose sanctions soon under law tightening restrictions against Moscow
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 14. /TASS/. The Washington administration is unlikely to impose new sanctions in the near future under the law tightening restrictions on Russia, the Politico newspaper wrote, citing sources.

On September 18, US President Donald Trump signed a bill passed by Congress that provides for sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership and state-owned companies, as well as secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners. "The legislation requires that 30 days after the bill’s signing, President Donald Trump must make a determination about what people and entities he characterizes as meeting the criteria for getting sanctioned. But, as critics of the bill pointed out before its passage, the legislation also includes broad waiver authority for the White House: The president just needs to submit a document to Congress saying a waiver ‘is in the national interests of the United States’," according to the publication.

"It’s a low bar for them to just send the waiver," a Democratic Senate aide told the newspaper. "I expect that that’s what would happen, and then there would be no recourse because that’s how the bill was written," he added.

Traditionally, if the administration was planning big sanctions steps, there would be a lot of messaging from the Treasury, State and Commerce departments in the leadup, the Senate aide said. That isn’t happening now, he noted.
news.summary: A Democratic Senate aide told Politico that the administration is showing no signs of readiness through Treasury, State and Commerce department channels

news.text:
WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will depart on Saturday ​on a five-day trip to India and Uzbekistan, the State Department ​said, adding that he will discuss energy cooperation in India.

Rubio ⁠will travel to Samarkand in Uzbekistan and to Mumbai and Jamnagar in India, ​the State Department said in a statement on Tuesday.

In India, Rubio will meet government ​officials to “exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation,” the statement said.

Indian and American officials indicated earlier this month that long-running efforts to finalize ​a bilateral trade agreement have stalled again.

US-India ties have been rocky this past year over ​issues including President Donald Trump’s repeated claim of brokering an India-Pakistan ceasefire and a US military attack ‌on ⁠a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers.

New Delhi has also raised concerns over US legislation allowing Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that purchase Russian energy, part of Washington’s efforts to pressure Moscow ​over its invasion of ​Ukraine.

India only briefly ⁠reduced purchases from Russia in early 2026 but they have since jumped, especially since the supply shock that followed ​the US-Israeli war on Iran.

The announcement of Rubio’s visit also comes ​during ongoing ⁠protests in India over the removal of 130 million voters from electoral rolls. Washington has thus far not commented on the demonstrations.

In Uzbekistan, Rubio will participate in ⁠bilateral engagements ​with officials from Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan ​and Kyrgyzstan, and lead a delegation of over 200 business leaders, the State Department said.

news.title: Trump predicts new Great Depression for US if Democrats win November elections
news.text:
NEW YORK, October 14. /TASS/. The US will face a new Great Depression if the Democrats win the midterm elections to Congress in November, US leader Donald Trump said.

"If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929-style economic depression," he said, speaking to supporters in Alaska. "If the Republicans win, you will each receive $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country, the likes of which we have never seen before," Trump added.

The Great Depression was a worldwide economic downturn that began in 1929 with the stock market crash in the United States and lasted until about 1939. news.title: New White House press secretary’s short and awkward first briefing brutally compared to 'hostage video'
news.text:
New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia faced immediate online ridicule following a shaky, 14-minute briefing debut that viewers brutally compared to a "hostage video."

Zacharia, who stepped up to the podium on Tuesday to replace former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, appeared visibly rattled and out of breath throughout her first appearance before the White House press corps.

Rather than establishing an authoritative command of the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, the newcomer spent the majority of her brief appearance reading directly from prepared speaking notes before fielding questions from a handpicked selection of friendly reporters.

The awkward 14-minute debut quickly unraveled on social media, where viewers pointed out Zacharia’s rapid breathing, stiff posture, and anxious delivery.

"Thought this was a hostage video," one viral post on X remarked alongside a clip of the briefing, while another commented: "She is already out of breath. Katie Zacharia starts off clearly (but understandably) nervous."

The most excruciating moment of the briefing arrived when Zacharia attempted to address a question regarding how she balances the grueling demands of the West Wing press office with raising her four young children.

Visibly flustered, the new press chief committed a glaring verbal slip-up, confusing her spouse with the commander-in-chief on live television.

"I love being with my kids. The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia told reporters. "So my president – excuse me, my husband – that's a good one."

The awkward Freudian slip drew nervous chuckles from the assembled media, prompting Zacharia to hurriedly recover by praising Donald Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had."

The briefing ended abruptly shortly thereafter. Over the course of the lightning-fast 14 minutes, Zacharia called upon just three journalists—restricting questions exclusively to conservative outlets Breitbart, Fox News, and the Daily Mail—before packing her notes and walking away from the podium without engaging the wider briefing room.

Zacharia, an attorney and former conservative commentator, faces an uphill climb stepping into the role just weeks ahead of high-stakes midterm elections.

Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, was known for combative, rapid-fire sparring sessions with mainstream network correspondents, leaving observers stunned by the stark contrast in energy and confidence during Zacharia's tentative premiere.

Political commentators and digital creators seized on the truncated conference as evidence of an administration eager to shield its newest spokesperson from rigorous press scrutiny.

As the video continued circulating across TikTok and X, critics argued that restricting questions and fleeing the room after under a quarter of an hour did little to dispel concerns over her readiness for the highest-pressure lectern in American politics.

Even a White House official chimed in. “Getting behind the podium is tough, but she got off on the wrong foot. She needs to get much better, fast, otherwise she'll break Scaramucci's record,” the official told MSNOW.

Meanwhile several commenters compared her performance to former press secretary Anthony Scaramucci who infamously only lasted 10 days in the post.

“She may not make it a full Scaramucci…” quipped one user online.

However, some commentators were far more forgiving, with Communications director Steven Cheung offering words of support and praise to the new recruit. “She commanded the room and effectively reminded the American people of all the great work President Trump and his Administration has done thus far,” Cheung wrote on X.

Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet also weighed in and said that Zacharia got off to a “solid start” but acknowledged her nerves may have gotten the better of her.

“Thought it was smart of new WH Press Sec Katie Zacharia to rip the band-aid and hold her first press briefing straight away. She came off perhaps a bit nervous reading the prepared statement, but very relatable and likeable,” he said. “She lit up when talking when about her family.”

President Trump meanwhile was perfectly happy with her performance stating: “I thought she did excellent. She did very good,"
news.summary: The tense 14-minute first briefing drew comparisons to a 'hostage video' as she abruptly fled the podium after three questions
news.author: Phoebe Tonks

news.title: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say
news.text:
DUBAI/LONDON/WASHINGTON: Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks ​to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.

Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US ‌and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.

Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.

The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its ​restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.

The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with ​one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.

“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring ⁠down global oil prices,” one of the two officials said.

The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials ​said.

Iran using spotters

A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started ​using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said.

Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it.

There were no casualties, the US official said.

Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through ​the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy.

The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November’s midterm elections, which will decide control of ​Congress.

US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.

The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure ‌on Tehran to ⁠reach a deal to end the conflict.

The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.

In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.

There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, ​pointing to a new escalation, according to data from ​the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.

“There ⁠is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.

Attacks over an expanded area

As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.

Analysis by maritime security sources based on ​attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the ​Strait of Hormuz, including waters off ⁠the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.

The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.

“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said.

“Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz.”

The Pentagon and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did ⁠not immediately respond ​to requests for comment.

Complete closure of Hormuz soon, says Iranian official

Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which ​no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. “It will be complete closure soon,” one of the officials said.

In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of ​Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level.

“IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said.

news.title: Trump promises $5,000 to every adult if Republicans win Congress
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 14 (IANS) US President Donald Trump promised every adult American citizen $5,000 if Republicans keep control of both chambers of Congress, telling a midterm rally in Wasilla, Alaska, that tariff revenue would pay for it. "If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate, I'm going to give all adult citizens in the United States $5,000. And only Republicans can do that because the Democrats can't, because we're taking in massive amounts of money," Trump said, adding that the money came from tariffs. He said "the Trump dividend that you get must be spent in the United States of America". He repeated the pledge at the end of the speech. Trump did not say how the payments would be made, when, or what they would cost. Any such payout would need Congress to approve it. "If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929 style economic depression," he said. The President was campaigning for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan three weeks before the November 3 elections. He called Democrat Mary Peltola "no show Mary". Early voting begins on October 19. On Iran, Trump said Tehran "will not have a nuclear weapon" and that the war "is going to end very soon and when it does, your prices are going to come tumbling down". "We opened the Straits," he said. "We've been taking more oil out of the Straits now than we did before the war started, believe it or not. We control the Straits." "Wait till you see what we do to Iran, because we sort of had it, you know, we've had it," he said, without giving details. On stage, Trump granted a full pardon to Mark Spurlock and signed pardons for two Anchorage diesel mechanics, Zachary Schubach and Patrick Fleming, who had been convicted of Clean Air Act violations for modifying vehicle emissions controls. "They want to put them in jail for ten years because they fixed an engine," Trump said. Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr told the rally the Commission "will vote this month to invest an additional $162 million to expand high speed internet in Alaska". Trump attacked Canada, saying "they have ripped us off for years but no longer", and accused Democrats of allowing "25 million people to pour across our borders". He did not back up the figure. He spoke at the Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center. His two-day trip also takes him to Nevada, Arizona and Montana. Fuel prices have become a central issue in the campaign, and Gulf tensions keep pressure on oil markets that India watches closely.

news.title: Trump went all the way to Alaska in a sign of how close its US Senate race may be
news.text: WASILLA: It's a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles (72 kilometers) north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called "one of the best and most respected senators in D.C." Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put "Alaska first" and emphasizing cost-of-living issues.During Tuesday's rally, Trump announced that Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project that he has been highlighting amid Sullivan's campaign and that it would invest more than $4 billion. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. The White House did not immediately provide further details.Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. And he announced pardons for two men who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations for tampering with federally mandated monitoring devices on certain vehicles..Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedlyDemocrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn't elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn't vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson's landslide 1964 reelection.Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump's approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets.Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally. That means the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him."The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen.The Trump administration has prioritized expanding oil and gas drilling in the state. Vice President JD Vance last week campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan and Republican Rep. Nick Begich.Sullivan recently joined Trump in the Oval Office, where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into the proposed Alaska gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized.Versions of a gas project have been proposed in Alaska for decades.Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan's home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support for the incumbent.Trump last campaigned in Alaska to try to defeat fellow RepublicanAlaska is home to around 740,000 people, making it slightly less populous than Denver. It ranks 48th out of 50 states in population, smaller than all but Vermont and Wyoming.Trump nonetheless headlined a 2022 rally in Anchorage opposing Republican Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski after she voted to convict him on a charge of incitement of insurrection during his second impeachment trial, following the attack on the US Capitol by a mob of his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, who challenged Murkowski that year, but that didn't stop incumbent Murkowski from winning reelection.In Wasilla, Max Christensen was waiting in line for the rally and said he hoped to hear more specifics from Trump about the natural gas project, and said he was "really curious just to see how he's going to handle things like inflation and gas prices and things like that."Christensen, 22, said he thinks Trump has been a great president "despite all his flaws and stuff," adding, "I think he really does genuinely care about the people of the United States of America.".This year, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballotTrump has complained about Alaska's unique elections system. The state has open primaries, in which the four top vote-getters — regardless of party affiliation — advance to the general election, which uses ranked choice voting.That's led to a scenario where there also will be another Dan Sullivan on the November ballot: retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whom Trump and other allies of Sen. Sullivan have called a sham candidate. Dan J. Sullivan has denied this, but Trump continued to hammer the other Sullivan at his rally. "They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get things a little confused," Trump said, as he repeatedly urged his supporters to vote for "the real Dan Sullivan."Trump also touted Begich, who is facing a competitive challenge from Bill Hill, an independent.Alaska has a history of rewarding candidates with an independent streak — something Vance acknowledged during his trip to Fairbanks last week."In very deep red years, Alaska is competitive. In very deep blue years, Alaska is still competitive," Vance said. "I think it's just a reality of the politics of the state."Independence has been hard to find in the Republican Party, where Trump for years has had total control. Some Republicans facing tough elections have begun tiptoeing away from the president on key issues such as Iran and tariffs, but not Sullivan, who has been vocal in supporting both.Trump also questioned why three Republicans were running against a Democrat for governor and endorsed Bernadette Wilson, who finished third in the August primary but was the top vote-getting Republican. Mike Dunleavy — are urging voters to rank Republicans on the ballot.Many Republicans — despite reservations with ranked voting — have seen a ranking strategy in that race as crucial for Republicans trying to win the seat.Trump's trade war with Canada may also be a factorTrump has also triggered a trade war with Canada, which shares a 1,500-plus-mile (2,450-kilometer) border with Alaska and is among the state's most important trading partners.The US banned nearly $1 billion worth of imports from its neighbor — including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles — after previously imposing 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian products. news.title: Russian diesel not for us, but for world markets: Trump
news.text:
Facing criticism over the diesel deal with Russia, US President Donald Trump said the fuel from Moscow’s refineries was meant to stabilise the global market, which has been hit by high prices.

On October 9, Trump announced that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”

To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel shipments to global markets until April 7, 2027.

The move came ahead of November congressional midterms in the US, as diesel prices surged amid supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.

“That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us,” Trump told reporters here on Tuesday, amid a growing chorus against the surprise deal he announced last week after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Republicans and Democrats hit out at the deal, which Trump announced three weeks after the US Congress authorised him to impose sweeping sanctions on Russia and slapped tariffs on its key trading partners, including China and India.

“That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices. And when you knock out diesel refineries, that’s not a great thing. But they are not releasing it to us. They are releasing it to the entire world,” Trump said.

On Tuesday, a bipartisan group of US senators wrote to Trump, terming the Russia deal a “gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies”.

“The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9 will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans,” the senators said.

The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse and Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," the letter said.

Senators said they recognised the need to lower energy costs for Americans, but asserted that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans.

The deal “only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians,” they said.

“It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea,” the senators said.

Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump swiftly signed into law.

“Both chambers passed the legislation with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent and granting you the authorities to broker a just and fair peace,” the senators said.

They said these authorities require the president to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, particularly China, thereby enhancing the US negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict.

 Arsenal cruise past Lille into share of Champions League lead 







LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP)—Arsenal blew away Lille with a three-goal blitz in seven second-half minutes for a 3-0 win to extend their perfect start to the Champions League.

Jurrien Timber’s deft finish opened the floodgates just after the hour at the Emirates Stadium before Eberechi Eze and Bukayo Saka rounded off the scoring.

Victory takes Arsenal into a share of the lead at the top of the Champions League table alongside Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon.

Mikel Arteta was able to use the wealth of resources at his disposal as he made five changes to the side that beat Leeds 2-1 on Saturday.

But it was Lille boss Davide Ancelotti, son of Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti, who was the happier after a goalless first half.

The visitors even had the ball in the net but Ayase Ueda was flagged offside.

Bruno Guimaraes came closest to breaking the deadlock for Arsenal before the break when he fired wide from close range and then his powerful shot from range was parried by Berke Ozer.

The Gunners quickly went through the gears in the second period once Timber dinked the ball over Ozer from Noni Madueke’s pass.

Arteta had left arguably his three most potent attacking weapons on the bench and the introduction of Saka, Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard made an immediate impact.

“The ones that finish the game are extraordinary,” said Arteta.

“They increase the intensity, the quality and we suffocate them more and more and more.”

Saka’s low cross picked out Eze whose deflected shot flew into the top corner to end any doubt over the destiny of the three points.

The England winger then finished off an exquisite team move from Havertz’s cut-back for Arsenal’s third.

There were further cheers from the home fans when Olivier Giroud came on as a late substitute for Lille on his return to the club where he scored 105 goals in a six-year spell.

But Giroud could not conjure up another Emirates goal as Lille remain without a Champions League point after defeat to Real Betis on matchday one.

news.title: US may have ‘gone too far’ in targeting Iran leaders
news.text:
OHIO: US President Donald Trump said that the United States “might have gone too far” in targeting Iran’s leadership.

“We might have gone too far with the leaders because we don’t know who the hell we’re dealing with any more,” he said during a campaign rally in Ohio, according to Middle East Eye.

“Nobody wants to be the president of Iran,” he added, claiming that potential candidates did not want to take up the position. Trump made this remark despite Masoud Pezeshkian being Iran’s president since July 2024.

“We’re having a hard time figuring out who the hell to deal with, to be honest with you. I think we went too far,” the US president said.

Trump says he doesn’t believe China, Russia are helping Iran

Meanwhile, Trump said on Monday that he does not believe that China and Russia are helping Iran, adding that they have “too much to lose.”

Trump has faced pressure over reports that Chinese and Russian entities have supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.

Responding to comments that China and Russia are helping Iran, Trump said in a post on Truth Social: “If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!”

Trump said in July that he did not believe China and Russia were selling weapons to Iran, warning that “it would be very bad for them” if they did.

China and Russia both maintain strong ties with Iran but have refrained from getting directly involved in the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

Since the outbreak of the war, Russia has sent humanitarian aid to Iran, but has otherwise not officially announced any concrete assistance.

The Kremlin has denied US media reports claiming that Moscow passed sensitive intelligence to Iran, including the locations of US warships and aircraft in the region.

China has sharply condemned US and Israeli strikes while also criticising Iranian attacks on Gulf states and the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.

China has previously supplied Iran with drones as well as equipment that can be used for both civilian and military purposes.

Beijing has denied reports that the country’s top semiconductor firm, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, has sent chipmaking tools to Iran.

China and Russia have also been accused of helping Iran circumvent international sanctions targeting its oil sales.

Trump has frequently taken a more deferential tone toward Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin than he has toward some of Washington’s own allies, saying that they must be respected as the leaders of major world powers.

Published in Dawn, October 14th, 2026

news.title: Houthis warn of ‘painful’ response as Saudis strike Yemen fuel sites
news.text:
Coalition says struck sites ‘supported Houthi missile, drone operations’• Aerial threat alerts issued for Riyadh, Eastern Province; blasts heard near Dhahran• Trump warns rebels; Erdogan pledges support for Riyadh

RIYADH: Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen on Tuesday, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a “harsh and painful” response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations.

Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom’s Eastern Province and Riyadh. Residents in the Eastern Province received alerts saying the area faced a “hostile aerial threat” before being told shortly afterwards that the danger had passed.

Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. There was no immediate confirmation that the facility itself had been struck. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments from an intercepted projectile had fallen on a residential area in Dhahran.

The developments marked a further escalation in the rapidly widening confrontation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, who have stepped up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom over the past week.

Earlier on Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had conducted military operations against “vital assets” used by the Houthis to sustain their war effort, Al Jazeera reported.

Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said the targets included the Al-Sabaha central station in Sanaa, underground fuel reserves and storage tanks, as well as energy facilities in Hodeidah, Sanaa and Dhamar.

The coalition said the sites were being used to supply the Houthis’ missile and drone arsenal, posing threats to Saudi Arabia, airports, ports and commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

“The operation aims to neutralise the Houthis’ capabilities that threaten the Kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea, and waterways,” the coalition said.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had struck a Yemen Petroleum Company facility on the western outskirts of Sanaa.

An AFP correspondent in the Yemeni capital reported hearing an explosion after the coalition had earlier issued an evacuation warning for civilians near the site — its first such order for Sanaa since the war flared up again.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree also said the site had “no military value”, while the group warned that any further Saudi strikes would draw retaliation against targets in the kingdom.

The Houthis identified Riyadh’s international airport, an oil refinery in the capital and Aramco facilities in eastern Saudi Arabia among potential targets, and renewed warnings to workers to stay away from sites that could be attacked.

Saudi Arabia vows response

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the kingdom would not allow threats to its security or to freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.

It warned that the Houthis would “face the consequences of their crimes and repeated attacks” on Saudi airports, holy cities and economic facilities.

Saudi Arabia also faced continuing attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying it had intercepted three drones north of Riyadh.

Blasts had also been heard over the Saudi capital late on Monday, when the coalition said it intercepted a Houthi missile and the group claimed another attack on Riyadh airport.

Trump, Erdogan weigh in US President Donald Trump spoke to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday and later told reporters that the Houthis were “behaving very badly”.

He also accused the group of trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections and warned that he would “never forget” their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Trump said he might ask Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.

Earlier on Tuesday, Erdogan told the Sa--u--di crown prince that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, according to the Turkish presidency, though no details were given on any specific new line of support.

Turkiye and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, although Ankara still requires parliamentary approval to implement its commitments under the agreement.

Senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti said the group would target American interests in the region if Washington joined the war.

He said the attacks on Saudi targets were intended to signal to the Saudi leadership that it could no longer wage war in Yemen “from a safe position”.

news.title: Iran shifts tactics, steps up ship attacks to pressure Trump before US midterms
news.text: Iran is changing its tactics to step up attacks on commercial shipping in the Gulf and keep global oil prices elevated ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. This comes as Tehran seeks to increase economic pressure on US President Donald Trump.“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” news agency Reuters quoted one Iranian official saying. The official added that the strategy had been approved at the highest levels of Iran's leadership.The official said Tehran would seek to push prices higher whenever Washington appeared close to bringing them down.“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the official told Reuters, describing the campaign as an effort to undermine Trump's attempts to ease energy costs before voters go to the polls.The tactical change involves the use of unarmed spotters in small boats by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels.A US military official told Reuters that the tactic emerged after US strikes damaged much of Iran's radar capabilities. In a previously unreported incident, US forces identified spotters operating from a traditional dhow and relaying targeting information to the IRGC.The Iranian officials also said Iran intended to expand its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, including areas off Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.“Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz,” the official said, warning that ships violating Iran's restrictions could face threats beyond the strategic waterway.The strategy could complicate Trump's efforts to ease energy costs ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which control of Congress is at stake.Sustained disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could keep oil prices elevated, increasing fuel costs for American consumers and adding to economic pressure on the administration.Higher energy prices could also give Trump's political opponents an opportunity to criticise his handling of the conflict and its economic consequences.You use AI every day. This tactic is designed to apply economic pressure on the United States and its allies, complicating their strategies just ahead of the midterm elections. As tensions rise, the risk to multiple vessels may increase, potentially affecting energy costs for American consumers.

news.title: Trump pardons Alaskan mechanics from Biden-era emissions case
news.text:
President Donald Trump says he's pardoning the owners of a vehicle repair shop in Alaska who were accused of tampering with federally-mandated monitoring devices and removing required air pollution control equipment from dozens of vehicles.

The owners of Arm Rippin Toys, Inc., in Anchorage plead guilty in 2022 to one count of violating the Clean Air Act, according to the Biden-era Justice Department.

Trump brought two of the company's owners, Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming, to the stage on Oct. 13 at his Wasilla, Alaska, rally in support of Republican candidates competing in November elections and said he was immediately pardoning the mechanics.

The president said that was also taking care of a third co-owner of the company, Michael Hanzuk, as he signed documents provided to him by an aide.

Trump said the men were convicted "because they fixed an engine" and were facing 10 years in prison.

"The concept is that if you allow people to fix the engine, they're going to take all of the environmental crap that makes it bad, makes it inefficient, makes it expensive, that they're going to undo that. And when you undo that, you therefore send fumes into the air," Trump declared. "Well, I heard about it. I read the story about it and did a little check in, and I'm giving each one of the three an unconditional pardon."

The U.S. Attorney's office said in 2022 that the company's co-owners and employees "falsified, tampered with and rendered inaccurate" emissions monitoring devices on at least 37 vehicles between July 2019 and September 2020. Arm Rippin Toys collected some $100,000 for conducting the unlawful service on diesel vehicles.

Hanzuk and Czubak were sentenced to five years probation, community service and ordered to pay a $66,000 fine.

At the Oct. 13 rally, Czubak said thanked Trump for clearing their record and told the crowd: "It destroyed friendships. It destroyed families. We're not criminals. We're not trying to hurt anybody. We want to help Alaskans. We want to help people with diesel trucks, vehicles across the world. "

In his remarks, Trump referred to a pardon he gave another Alaskan diesel mechanic in separate emissions case in July and accused the Biden administration of "viciously targeted the Alaskan way of life."

news.title: Two Nights Without Missile Warnings – Zelensky Raises Alarm as Trump Denies Intelligence Cutoff
news.text:
For two consecutive nights, the air raid warnings that normally give Kyiv residents precious time to seek shelter came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the Ukrainian capital.

On Monday and Tuesday, Oct. 12–13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, striking civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Ukraine received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

The second attack hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 thermal power plant and a nine-story residential building, killing at least two people and injuring 21, including a child.

Zelensky described Monday’s attack as “particularly vile,” saying five Russian ballistic missiles had struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv without advance warning from Ukraine’s partners.

“Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike,” Zelensky said Tuesday, Oct. 13.

“Advance intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches is critical to saving lives. Early warnings give people time to seek shelter and help prevent casualties.”

In his evening address, Zelensky revealed that Ukrainian forces had detected the five missiles only seconds before impact.

“Normally, we receive advance warnings from our partners, which are crucial for our defense,” Zelensky said, stressing that intelligence sharing helps Ukraine protect civilians and prevent Russian killings.

However, Zelensky did not specify which partner had failed to provide the warnings, nor did he explicitly accuse Washington of deliberately withholding intelligence.

The consequences were immediate for civilians.

A Kyiv Post journalist recounted how a friend, unaware of the incoming missiles, was walking her dog on Kyiv’s left bank when the attack began.

“The explosions were so loud that she was terrified,” the journalist said.

The intelligence question – a technical failure or political pressure?

The missing warnings come at an especially sensitive moment in US-Ukrainian relations.

According to an Axios report published Oct. 9, citing a Ukrainian official, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned during negotiations in Miami that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil refineries.

However, a US official denied that such a threat had been made, saying Washington remained a strong partner providing Ukraine with intelligence and weapons.

President Donald Trump rejected suggestions that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” Trump told reporters Tuesday, Oct. 13, adding that Washington was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the war.

Yet Trump’s assurances have not resolved the central question: why did Ukraine go two consecutive nights without the early missile warnings it normally receives from its Western partners?

The Trump administration’s response was less definitive when the question reached the White House briefing room on Tuesday.

Katie Zacharia, Trump’s newly appointed press secretary, was asked directly by Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy whether the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

“I’ll have to get back to you on that,” she replied during her first briefing.

Trump’s Russian diesel deal adds to questions

The intelligence concerns emerged just days after Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.

On Oct. 9, the US Treasury Department issued General License 135, authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel.

The temporary sanctions relief followed Trump’s agreement with Putin to release Russian diesel supplies onto international markets in an effort to ease rising fuel prices.

The decision has drawn criticism from lawmakers in Washington, who warn that renewed Russian energy revenues could help finance Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
news.summary: Ukraine received no advance allied warnings during Russian ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv on Oct. 12 and 13. Zelensky sounded the alarm without naming the country responsible. The failures followed an Axios report that US officials threatened to suspend intelligence sharing over Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Trump denied any cutoff, while his new press secretary said she would look into the matter.

news.title: Donald Trump Calls Iran a ‘Failed Country’, Says US Will Make Decision on Tehran Soon
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has described Iran as a “failed country” and said Washington will make a decision on Tehran “very soon”, as tensions between the two countries continue amid an ongoing conflict and stalled diplomatic efforts. Trump cited Iran’s economic difficulties and claimed that the government was struggling to pay its military personnel, but did not specify what action the United States was considering.

Trump Cites Iran’s Economic Crisis

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Tuesday, October 13, Trump criticised Iran’s economic condition and claimed that the country was facing extremely high inflation and financial difficulties.

news.title: Donald Trump calls heckler a 'spoiled child' at Alaska rally in on-stage outburst
news.text: President Donald Trump took a heckler to task during a rally in Alaska, as part of his campaign to bolster Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. As the president was discussing his 2024 triumph over former Vice President Kamala Harris, a disturbance could be heard amongst the crowd. "Sounds like we have a spoiled child," he commented, prompting boos from the audience. The camera swiftly swung towards the commotion, before quickly refocusing on Trump , who commended the police. "Wow, good law enforcement!" he exclaimed. Eventually, the camera caught sight of a man being ushered out of the Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center. "Wow, good job! Wow!" Trump applauded, reports the Mirror US . "He's now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father, who both voted for me by the way," the president remarked about the heckler. This follows a similar incident just yesterday in Youngstown, where a female heckler was punched in the face by a male attendee before security intervened to escort her from the event. During the scuffle, Trump referred to the woman as a "fat guy" who needs to "go on a diet." The woman, sporting a shirt reading "Release the Epstein files," was shoved to the floor by a male participant, struck in the face, and dragged by the hair. During the attack, the president branded the woman a "paid protester" who receives cash from "the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum." Echoing this latest episode, Trump declared the woman would be "going back home to mom," alleging that the demonstrator's parents likely backed him. "That's a very low-class protestor," he remarked. "What he doesn't know is his mother and father voted for me. He's going to get home and he's going to get smacked." In recent days, the president has staged events in Nebraska, Texas, New York, Tennessee, and Ohio to strengthen the GOP's prospects in fiercely competitive contests. The Wasilla gathering follows a comparable rally in Fairbanks last week headlined by Vice President JD Vance. The occasions were organised to drum up backing for Alaskan Sen. Dan Sullivan, who finds himself in a tight battle that may decide whether Republicans maintain Senate control following next month's midterms. Sullivan confronts opposition from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who secured more ballots than Sullivan in Alaska's open primary during August. Trump has traditionally been quite popular in Wasilla. The district backed him with over 75% of the vote in 2024. Trump clinched Alaska's presidential elections in 2016, 2020, and 2024, but recent surveys suggest his popularity in the state is on the decline.
news.summary: President Donald Trump called out a heckler while headlining a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday as part of his effort to boost Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections

news.title: Sen. Ed Markey and John Deaton square off in only debate before election
news.text:
In three weeks, Democratic incumbent Sen. Ed Markey and Republican John Deaton will face off on ballots across the commonwealth. But first, the two Senate candidates met in an antagonistic debate Tuesday evening — the only scheduled debate between the two before the Nov. 3 election.

The debate, hosted by WBZ-TV’s John Keller, pitted longtime politician Markey, 80, against a relative political newcomer in 59-year-old Deaton. The Republican nominee first entered the Massachusetts political scene in 2024, when he challenged Sen. Elizabeth Warren and lost by a nearly 20-point margin.

Deaton, a lawyer who specializes in representing asbestos poisoning victims and advocates for cryptocurrency, ran unopposed in the Republican primary earlier this year. Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton by nearly 30 points in the Sept. 1 Democratic primary.

According to late September polling by UNH, Markey is favored to defeat Deaton by 23 points to win what would be his third full term as senator. If Deaton were to win, he would be just the second Republican senator from the state to win since 1966 and the first since Scott Brown in 2010. 

Tuesday’s debate was headlined by Markey’s repeated attempts to cast Deaton as another GOP soldier for President Donald Trump’s agenda. The senator emphasized the importance of a Democratic majority in the Senate to place checks on the president. 

Deaton subsequently distanced himself from the MAGA base and painted himself as a bipartisan politician throughout the debate. His attacks centered on the progressive senator’s “extreme” positions and shortcomings in delivering promises across 50 years in Congress.

Here are 5 takeaways from Tuesday’s debate:

A focus on Donald Trump 

The candidates’ respective relationships to President Donald Trump proved to be the largest point of tension between the two.

Markey, who voted against 21 of Trump’s 22 cabinet appointees in 2025, positioned himself as a staunch opponent to the president during the debate. He strove to paint Deaton as nothing more than a cog to further Trump’s agenda.

Markey invoked the president’s name more than 40 times throughout the hour-long debate, including in the first sentence of his opening remarks.

“I’m going to Washington to be a check on Donald Trump. Mr. Deaton is going to Washington to be a blank check for Donald Trump,” Markey said in his opening statement. 

In a state where UNH polling shows nearly three-quarters of residents disapprove of the president, Markey’s messaging aligns with residents ahead of the midterm.

Deaton tried to paint the senator as giving broken-record responses that failed to address the Republican as a candidate.

“You notice how many times he talks about Trump, Trump, Trump,” Deaton said during the debate. He later added, “Senator, my God, … I’m John Deaton, and I’m the one that is debating you, not Donald Trump.”

Deaton has made his self-described distance from Trump and the Republican MAGA base a key point in his campaign. During the debate, Deaton said he has never endorsed or voted for the president. Deaton differs from the MAGA base on several key policies, as a pro-abortion rights, anti-Iran war candidate. 

A split on partisanship

Deaton has positioned himself as more of a bipartisan, independent candidate who would work with both sides of the aisle. But, he said, his opponent is a “partisan person,” who will not oppose anyone wearing a “Democrat jersey.” 

“I wear an American jersey. I call President Trump out. I’ll call a Democrat president out. We’ve got to stop hating each other and dividing each other,” Deaton said.

At one point in the debate, Deaton said he wished Markey was more open to working with the other side — he pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s relationship with the president.

“Mamdani calls Trump a fascist. He calls him a misogynist, a racist. But then he goes to Washington and works for New York City,” Deaton said. “Go to Washington and work for the people of Massachusetts, regardless if it’s Trump, regardless if it’s … AOC. I’ll do that.”

Markey said Deaton wants voters to believe in a “fantasy land,” where Republicans who buck the president’s agenda don’t face consequences from the MAGA base. He specifically pointed to Republican senators who opposed the president and either didn’t file for reelection or lost the following election, such as Thom Tillis and Bill Cassidy.

“Right out of Godfather Part One, [Trump] gives them each an offer they can’t refuse. If they don’t do what he wants, they’re out,” Markey said.

Markey characterized Deaton’s attempt to be both independent and a Republican as an “oxymoron.”

“The ‘R’ on your jersey, Mr. Deaton, will just stand for ‘rubber stamp’ if you go down there,” Markey said. “You will be in the majority, and Donald Trump and those Republicans will once again control every single committee.”

Career politicians and red herrings

In Deaton’s opening statement, he stressed that he isn’t running against the 80-year-old senator because of Markey’s age. However, he attacked various “regrets” throughout Markey’s 50-year career in Congress.

For example, he pointed to Markey’s support for a ban on abortion in the 1970s — a position Markey changed in 1983, according to The Boston Globe. He also pointed to Markey’s vote to authorize the Iraq war — a position the senator says he now regrets, according to WBUR.

“Senator Markey is just same old, same old, 53 years of trying to get it done. Never gets it done, even when his party’s in control,” Deaton said. 

Markey brushed off the attacks as “red herrings” meant to take away from the issues at the center of the election, such as rising prices for gas, food, electricity, and healthcare.

“It’s all about Trump’s policies, which have had a severe adverse impact on ordinary families watching this debate tonight,” Markey said. “If all it is is a continuation of business as usual … then they’re going to continue to suffer the way they are right now.”

Healthcare, energy, and AI

When it came to policy debate between the two candidates, there was a surprising amount of overlap in their positions. However, the two often differed in the means to get to those ends. 

Markey, a firm progressive, continued to push for Medicare for all throughout the debate. He cited a 2025 report by the Boston Public Health Commission which found a 23-year gap in life expectancy between Roxbury and Back Bay residents.

While Deaton said he supports more affordable health care, he called Markey’s position “extreme.” Deaton said he instead has a plan to break up the few “vertically integrated insurance companies” that control a majority of Americans’ healthcare. 

Both candidates supported various kinds of clean energy solutions. 

Markey said the Green New Deal, which he co-sponsored, led to 93 percent of electric generating capacity in the country coming from wind, solar, and battery storage — a finding reported by the U.S. Energy Information Administration in 2026.

Deaton said he supported a “multifaceted” approach to energy with a belief in solar and geothermal energy. He also emphasized his support for nuclear energy.

Both Markey and Deaton also supported safeguards around artificial intelligence.

Markey, who has introduced nearly a dozen bills to create safeguards around AI, was vehement about placing guardrails on the technology during the debate. He said AI regulations are currently handled by Silicon Valley billionaires and agreements between Trump and AI CEOs.

If reelected, Markey said a Democratic majority would call AI “bros” to testify in front of Congress and be held accountable.

Deaton acknowledged the potential advantages of AI, saying the technology could help end cancer or hunger, but he said he worries about elderly residents who can be “taken advantage of” by AI.

A second debate?

While Tuesday evening was the only scheduled debate between the two candidates, Deaton asked Markey for a second debate in western Massachusetts at the end of Tuesday’s debate.

“You’re a very good debater,” Deaton said. “Can we agree right now, Senator?”

Deaton held his hand out towards Markey, but the senator didn’t accept the invitation. 

“We have seen the clear differences between us,” Markey said. “The people of Massachusetts right now have had more than enough information given to them so they can make a decision on election day.”

Markey is favored to win by 23 points, according to late September polling by UNH.

news.title: US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog lawsuit seeking records on Elon Musk's DOGE
news.text:
APThe Supreme Court has agreed to hear a lawsuit concerning public records about Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency

Washington: The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear arguments in a watchdog's lawsuit seeking public records about billionaire Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency.The high court is intervening for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington's case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term. The Trump administration asked the court to hear the case.Last year, the high court reined in a district court's order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court's conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group.CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act.The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA's requirements as a presidential advisory body.Live EventsCooper ruled in CREW's favor and ordered expedited processing of the group's records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW.The Trump administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court's direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the "autonomy and confidentiality" of presidential advisers."Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA's reach," Justice Department attorneys wrote.The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorized the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason.CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court's previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025."Undisputed facts in the public record - including the President's statements - confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government," its attorneys wrote.In a statement Tuesday, CREW attorney Nikhel Sus said the lower courts have uniformly ruled that it is entitled to records that could help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to the Freedom of Information Act."We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration's efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government," Sus said in the statement.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

 Trump ousts Greece ambassador over ethics scandal 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—United States (US) President Donald Trump forced his ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, out of the administration on Tuesday, amid allegations that she sought money from one of his supporters and accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen.

“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters at her first White House briefing.

The announcement came a day after Trump acknowledged that he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

“She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump told reporters after the announcement, adding that he had not spoken to her, but that “she will not be there.”

In a statement on X, Guilfoyle rejected the allegations against her and defended her record as ambassador, highlighting efforts to boost US energy exports and strengthen security ties with Greece.

“These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she wrote.

Guilfoyle thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, pledging her continued loyalty to the president while acknowledging that her time as ambassador “may be coming to an end.”

Guilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny following a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal about her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy businessmen.

The newspaper reported that she asked Eric Deters, an influential Trump supporter, to pay off $100,000 in personal credit card debt shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.

She requested he complete the transaction through a wire transfer so as not to leave a paper trail, the paper said.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote to Deters in a message accompanied by instructions for paying her credit card company, according to the Journal, which published screenshots of the exchanges.

– Luxury trips –

Deters refused to make the payment, telling the newspaper that doing so would have cost him his marriage.

Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed the authenticity of the messages and denied wrongdoing.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek businessmen, citing hundreds of messages, emails and other records, including recorded conversations.

She traveled to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, aboard a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group, according to the newspaper.

Guilfoyle also spent Christmas at the exclusive Swiss ski resort of Gstaad with Greek shipping magnate Nikolas Tsakos, and stayed at a luxury Paris hotel on a trip with him, with Tsakos footing the bill, the Journal reported.

The State Department’s inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts, according to US media reports.

The revelations emerged as Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Europe last week, including a stop in Athens, where he declined to comment on the allegations.

Guilfoyle, a prominent figure in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, was appointed ambassador after her engagement to Donald Trump Jr. ended.

A former prosecutor and television commentator, she was previously married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom.
