news.title: As Russia turns to Asia, India a ‘natural option’ for Moscow beyond China, says EAM Jaishankar
news.text:
PTIIndia is natural option for Russia as Moscow turns to Asia, says Jaishankar

India is a natural option for Russia as Moscow turns increasingly towards Asia after its ties with Europe turned bitter, with New Delhi's relationship with Moscow staying steady for nearly eight decades.External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar made the remarks on Tuesday while speaking to John Micklethwait, Editor-in-Chief of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, in New Delhi. He said the Russia-Europe relationship had become "pretty much a broken, embittered relationship" since the Ukraine war.Also read: India-US trade deal heading towards ‘landing point’, EAM Jaishankar says"Historically, Russia has always seen itself as a European country. The result of what has happened because of the Ukraine war is that Russia, perforce, has turned much more to Asia. In Asia, much of that is towards China. But I do believe it's in our interest, and in the world's interest, that Russia has multiple choices and that it has other relationships in Asia of great weight and consequence," he said.Jaishankar said India had enjoyed decent ties with Russia from the early years and that these ties had stayed steady. "We are a natural option in that regard because we've had very decent relations with Russia from pretty much the early start... What we are doing right now is we are maintaining our relationship with Russia," he said.Live Events'We are reassuring Russia'The minister said India was reassuring Moscow that its ties with New Delhi remain steady even as the world and Russia's strategic calculations have changed."In my own words, we are reassuring Russia that while we understand today the world has changed, Russia has changed, the entire strategic calculation between Russia and Europe and Russia and the West has changed... We're not even passing a value judgment on it. All we are saying is that we, by maintaining our relationship, are reassuring Russia that something which has been built up over the last 75-80 years remains steady," he said.He added that the relationship had helped the balance of power in Asia. "It's an option that has worked for both of us. It has had a steady impact on the balance of power and overall status quo in Asia, and we think that's a good thing," he said.EU steps up pressure on RussiaHis remarks come as the European Union increases economic pressure on Russia over the war in Ukraine. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Monday announced nearly 1,600 sanctions listings against Russia's military-industrial complex and people linked to elections in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories."The main topic is war in Ukraine. We have now 1,600 listings that we are putting forward regarding the Russian military-industrial complex, but also the sham elections in Russia regarding the occupied territories of Ukraine," Kallas said.According to a European Council press release, the bloc adopted restrictive measures against 1,569 individuals and entities. These include 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals serving as chief executive officers of those companies. The latest package brings the total number of individuals and entities listed under the EU sanctions regime to nearly 4,600.The measures target companies that supply components used in advanced Russian weapons systems, including missiles, drones and aircraft. These components include semiconductors, microcircuits, computers, communication equipment, radar systems, explosives, ammunition, optics and navigation systems.The European Council said the measures respond to Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine, particularly attacks on civilian infrastructure. The sanctions announcement also came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy questioned Russia's intentions amid US President Donald Trump's push for an energy ceasefire.India-US trade deal 'heading towards a landing point'At the same forum, Jaishankar said negotiations on the India-US trade deal were heading towards a possible conclusion, with officials from both countries working to resolve outstanding issues.He said India was "pretty far advanced" in the process. "My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point," he said. He declined to share details, saying there were still "a few things" to resolve.Also read:'Engage America, manage China, cultivate Europe, & reassure Russia': Jaishankar lays out his foreign policy formulaJaishankar said the outcome would depend not only on the terms India and the US negotiate between themselves, but also on how those terms compare with deals Washington reaches with competing economies. "That part of it is not entirely clear because not everybody has worked out the deal," he said. He added that the US Trade Representative and India's Commerce and Industry Ministry were working to iron out the remaining issues.Explaining the wider context, he said the US had taken a different approach to tariffs as it sought to rebuild its industrial base. "The US is today determined to reindustrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy," he said. He added that major economies were negotiating with the US on these terms and India was not alone in the process.Jaishankar also said the underlying areas of convergence between India and the US had not fundamentally changed. He described the relationship as a strategic partnership rather than a formal alliance.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump biographer knows the 'real reason' Guilfoyle’s out — and it's not corruption
news.text:
Michael Wolff says he knows exactly why President Donald Trump fired Kimberly Guilfoyle, and it probably has very little to do with corruption. Corruption, he said, is the lifeblood of the Trump administration — so it’s not that.

Wolff is a longtime reporter and author, best known for his extensive coverage of Trump's political career, penning several books about his chaotic first term. But since Guilfoyle’s corruption is likely nothing compared to that of Trump, Wolff and co-host Joanna Coles discussed the real reason in the latest episode of his Daily Beast podcast, "Inside Trump's Head."

Kimberly Guilfoyle is a reflection of so much that goes on in Trump World. Donald Trump sets the model for [corruption],” Wolff told Coles. “We can't believe we've gotten into the position where we can effectively extort money from anybody.”

But to see the real reason for the Greek ambassador’s ejection the biographer said look no further than the woman’s likeability

“One of the answers is that she's low-hanging fruit, and the other is that the Trumps can't stand her,” said Wolff. “I think they've been asking this question for a long time: ‘how do we get rid of her? How did Don, Jr. ever end up with her?”

After praising her earlier in her career with the administration, Trump dismissed any meaningful connection to Guilfoyle after the former ambassador resigned in disgrace on Tuesday for allegedly misusing her office for personal profit. Trump gave Guilfoyle the cold shoulder, now describing Guilfoyle's engagement to his eldest son as "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”

But Wolff said Guilfoyle is all things Trump.

“It's an extraordinary story of the kind of the rank — if not comical — ambition possessed by so many people in the Trump world, as a matter of fact,” said Wolff, “so all of these revelations about her trying to get money from this person and trying to get money from that person … the truth is that almost everybody in the Trump orbit you could pin similar things on them. So, it would be interesting to see all of their emails.”

“But I think the other thing is that Kimberly Guilfoyle, in a world where everybody hates everybody, the person they hate the most is KG,” Wolff said.

Wolff argues that people around Trump mostly despise one another, but they reserve the most hate for Trump’s own privileged family. So, Guilfoyle’s tenure as a family member engendered “real animosity” for her throughout the administration.

“I was going to say there's nobody who has a positive word to say about Kimberly Guilfoyle, but it's worse than that,” said Wolff. “Everybody has the most terrible things to say about her.”

Wolff added that as a dirty dealer deep in the dirty deals of the Trump family’s grift, Guilfoyle probably has as much dirt on anybody, and Wolff said he would love to see her emails and texts.

“There was a moment actually in the earlier stages of her relationship with Don, Jr. when she went around saying that Trump had made a pass at her,” said Wolff. So Guilfoyle’s dirt was likely prolific, endless and very entertaining.

news.text:

"And then an official White House account, funded by taxpayers, reposts it. Will the American media finally report on the president’s manifest psychiatric disorders??"

The attacks against Ms. Comans were based entirely on false information' and many officials 'knew [they] were untrue.'"

To explain why Trump supporters display this behavior, Dr. Stephan Lewandowsky, a cognitive scientist and professor of cognitive science at the University of Bristol, spoke with AlterNet in August.

"If you look at internet trolls and their personality profiles, you find that they score very high on what's called the dark triad of personality: psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and [narcissism], that's what it's called," Lewandowsky told AlterNet. We do have it for trolls, though — I have data on that. People have published research on it, and the similarities are just overwhelming. So I'd be very surprised if these were well-adjusted, nice people."

He certainly would like to leave some monuments to himself in Washington. I don't think he'll be successful in knocking down the Kennedy Center. He'll certainly be successful at building that ballroom. It'll remain indeterminate about the Trump arc, the triumph. But Trump wants to name things after himself, he wants to make money, and he wants attention. So look to see those people restored to the White House, Politico, CNN."

news.title: Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica News
news.text:
The Caribbean country of Jamaica has received its first third-country deportations from the United States, as part of an expanding set of international agreements under President Donald Trump.

On Tuesday, 22 deportees from the US arrived at Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston, Jamaica.

Media reports indicate they were subsequently boarded onto a bus and taken to an undisclosed location.

Such deportations – which often involve non-citizens who have no ties to their destinations – have faced widespread condemnation from human rights groups and advocates who have questioned their legality.

But Jamaica is among a growing number of countries to accept third-country deportations, as part of Trump’s effort to implement the largest mass deportation campaign in US history.

At least 35 countries have entered into third-country deportation agreements with the US, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, an advocacy project affiliated with the groups Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The Washington Post reported last month that the Trump administration has earmarked roughly $410m to support such efforts.

Jamaica signed a bilateral memorandum of understanding in June to receive third-country deportations. Under the plan, Jamaica will transfer any deportees to their home countries or other destinations after their arrival.

The country’s government has also pledged not to accept any deportees with criminal records.

“The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries,” Jamaica’s Ministry of National Security and Peace and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade said in a joint statement.

It added that care for the deportees will be supported by the International Organization for Migration, a United Nations organisation.

“The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica,” the joint statement added.

Opposition leaders in Jamaica, however, spoke out against the deportation, framing the deal as a threat to the island’s security. They also questioned why the agreement had not been debated publicly.

“Jamaicans are being asked to trust a secret document that touches their security, their communities and their public services,” said Fitz Jackson, the opposition spokesperson on national security.

In response to Jackson’s statement, Foreign Minister Kamina Johnson Smith argued that any questions about the deportation deal “have all been answered”. She also indicated that the US has not agreed to make the deal public.

“As I explained before, some countries have agreed to receive criminals, we have not,” she wrote on social media.

“Some countries have had their agreements made public, but our partner has not agreed for this one to be.”

Legal challenges against the third-country deportations are ongoing in the US, where advocates have argued that deportees are being removed from the country without due process of law, the constitutional right to a fair hearing.

Critics have also argued that third-country deportations sometimes send immigrants to countries where they may face danger.

Some of the recipient countries, such as South Sudan, are in the midst of ongoing conflict or have faced accusations of serious human rights abuses.

Opponents have even said the third-country deportations are being used as a backdoor method for circumventing court protection orders.

Such orders may prohibit the US government from returning certain immigrants to their home countries, for fear of violence and persecution.

But by sending immigrants to third countries, critics say the Trump administration avoids violating such protection orders – though in some cases, the third country has then returned the deportee to the country identified in the US protection order.

In a February report by Democrats on the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, one official said anonymously that the purpose of such far-flung deportations was to instil fear.

“The point is that the administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere,” the official said. “The point is to scare people.”

news.title: US Secretary of State Rubio to travel to Uzbekistan, India from Oct 17-22
news.text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to India next week to further strengthen energy cooperation, the Department of State said on Tuesday.

Rubio will first visit Samarkand in Uzbekistan, and will then travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar in India from October 17-22, it said.

This will be Rubio’s second visit to India since May, when he attended the Quad Foreign Ministers’ meeting hosted by External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in New Delhi.

“He will meet with senior government officials to strengthen the US-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation,” the State Department said.

Rubio will also meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation, it said.

Rubio’s visit to Jamnagar is crucial as it is home to Reliance’s refinery, the world’s largest single-site facility with a capacity to process 1.4 million barrels per day of crude oil.

In March, President Donald Trump announced that the US will build its first refinery in 50 years with investment from Reliance Industries.

The refinery will come up at Brownsville in Texas at a cost of USD 300 billion, Trump said.

In Samarkand, Rubio will participate in the C5+1 Ministerial to highlight how strategic cooperation through this diplomatic platform promotes a more peaceful and prosperous future for the United States and the countries of Central Asia.

The Secretary will also participate in bilateral engagements with senior officials from all C5 countries -- Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Kyrgyz Republic.

A US commercial delegation comprising over 200 business leaders will accompany Rubio, ushering in a new era of strengthened commercial cooperation for the United States and Central Asia.

The planned livestream execution of the Fort Hood mass shooter is a “grotesque” work of “arrogant f--k” Pete Hegseth, broadcaster Chuck Todd said Tuesday. 

Todd, the former Meet the Press moderator, said on The Chuck ToddCast that livestreaming Nidal Hasan’s execution on Dec. 3 is “perhaps the most disturbing thing anybody out of the Trump orbit has proposed.”

“Nobody should mistake what I’m about to say as any sort of sympathy for Hasan, or any attempt to minimize what he did. He needs to rot in a hole for what he did,” Todd said of the 56-year-old former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009. “But what exactly is the purpose of turning his execution into a public spectacle?”

“Apparently, it’s just an obsession or a fascination with just demonstrating power: ‘Look at the power we have.’ So what, you arrogant f---? Pardon my language, but I just… this is grotesque.”

“I keep thinking about the dystopian movies from the ’80s, right?” Todd said, citing The Running Man. “Where society becomes so degraded that state sponsored violence is turned into mass entertainment—is this what Pete Hegseth grew up watching and idolizing? Man, what a broken mind.”

“When you see somebody who’s not just incompetent but, like, is defiantly incompetent and so broken and all these things—I mean, he needs help. He clearly does, because if you’re thinking this way—imagine thinking that there’s an audience for this. Who does he believe wants to watch the government execute somebody? What’s wrong with his mind that he wants to show this and see this?”

If it’s the Republican base that finds it appealing, then “think about what that assumption says about how this administration views its own supporters,” Todd said.

“I know plenty of people who voted for Donald Trump,” Todd said, “but I don’t believe these people signed up to watch the government execute prisoners and wanted the Defense secretary to become a snuff film producer.”

news.title: Georgia Senate debate takeaways: Ossoff shoos off interest in WH bid
news.text:
For the second time in less than a week Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff aggressively jousted with Republican challenger Mike Collins, who is struggling to keep Georgia's critical U.S. Senate race competitive.

Both contenders came out swinging during the Oct. 13 encounter much like they did five days prior when they exchanged personal insults while sharing policy contrasts.

Ossoff used the forum to grill Collins about his support for unpopular parts of President Donald Trump's agenda, condemning his opponent for refusing to publicly concede who won the 2020 election results and for hiring campaign aides with a history of expressing racist and antisemitic views.

But the 39-year-old Democrat mostly pounced on how the administration's trade war has helped raise prices.

"Folks are going to the grocery store; they're paying more than ever to stock their fridge," Ossoff said.

The hourlong debate, hosted by the Atlanta Press Club, also touched on immigration, voting rights and if Democrats would impeach Trump for a third time should they retake Congress.

Ossoff entered the midterm cycle as the only Senate Democrat seeking reelection in a state Trump won in 2024, which had many political observers initially casting him as the most vulnerable Democrat in the midterm cycle.

But that narrative has faded from headlines starting with Georgia Republicans failing to recruit Gov. Brian Kemp, a popular figure, to run for the seat. Collins is trailing by as much as 13 percentage points in some polls.

Democrats are now eagerly watching the race largely over speculation that Ossoff could run for president in 2028, citing the Peach State's pivotal battleground status and rising national profile due to viral takedowns of the Trump administration.

"What Ossoff has shown in his political career by winning a seat in Georgia is that he can speak to a diverse group of voters, whether that's Democrats or Republicans, and so I think that if he wins this race, he will be considered a serious presidential contender," Rotimi Adeoye, a Democratic comms strategist, told USA TODAY in June.

Here are the key moments from Tuesday's debate:

Running for president: Ossoff pledges to serve out term

The first question didn't avoid a conversation that's been orbiting Ossoff for months — will he seek the White House in two years?

Back in August, a national poll from Emerson College showed Ossoff leading Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a hypothetical matchup.

More recent surveys have Georgia's first Jewish senator among the top five Democrats in a potential presidential primary with about 8% behind Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

But when asked if he will serve a full six-year term if reelected, Ossoff expressed having "zero interest" in running for president in 2028.

"I'm running for re-election to the Senate, and tonight the contrast could not be clearer between these two Senate candidates," Ossoff said.

'I'm a little tired of this': Ossoff, Collins gets testy over racist ties

Much like during the first clash, Ossoff and Collins' exchange turned personal when the conversation focused on the Republican congressman's record of hiring campaign aides with a history of espousing anti-Black and antisemitic views.

"I condemn any sort of hate speech, anti-Semitism, hate of any kind (and) it's abhorrent," Collins said when asked if he were a white nationalist.

The GOP nominee immediately pivoted to spotlighting Ossoff's support for other Senate candidates, such as Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, and accused his Democratic rival of having a connection to influencer Hassan Piker, a popular left-wing activist who has become a lightning rod in the 2026 midterms for several controversial online comments.

Ossoff did not relent, however, once again mentioning that Collins' son-in-law reportedly shares neo-Nazi imagery online. He called Collins a "weak" person and asked the congressman to promise it would no longer "be produced" from his home.

In a 30-second rebuttal, Collins called out how a New York man was arrested for threatening to kill him and his son-in-law, which he said was due to Ossoff's comments. "I'm a little tired of this," he said.

Ossoff seeks to yoke Collins to Trump's trade war

Over and over again Ossoff reminded viewers how much prices have gone up and connected those costs to the Trump administration's trade war and other policy choices.

"Ground beef is up 30% since Donald Trump took office," Ossoff said. "Coffee is up 30% since Donald Trump took office, those were your votes. Tariffs you supported last week. You said the tariffs were making things fair, and I think that you should explain to Georgia voters why you voted for the tariffs and what you mean by that."

Collins, who is endorsed by Trump, at one point conceded "diesel prices are high." AAA reports the average gallon of diesel is $5.74. But the GOP congressman said, "supply is coming," slamming Ossoff for supporting mass transit and other environmental regulations.

"If it wasn't so, he wouldn't have voted for that Green New Deal. If it wasn't so, they wouldn't have killed the Keystone Pipeline," Collins said. "If it wasn't so, they'd be helping to to get us to where we're energy independent." He voted against that."

Rivals differ slightly over AI amid growing fears

The rise of artificial intelligence has unified voters with polls showing more Americans opposing than favoring construction of data centers in their areas.

Asked about the role of AI in the country's future, Ossoff called it the "most complex and important legislative question of our time." He called for federal inspectors and the fortification of the federal system in defense from bioterrorism.

"We have to recognize that we cannot allow the Trump administration, which is opposed to any regulation whatsoever, to put jobs at risk or our national security at risk," Ossoff said.

On Sept. 29 Trump convened six major technology companies who signed a joint commitment meant to self-regulate the safe development of AI.

Collins emphasized that the United States is in a race with China over the technology, which he said is already in many American's lives. He said if voters don't want data centers, he's oppose to the development, but would favor them being built if a community wanted one.

"The problem is there's a lot of bad actors out there in anything that you have," Collins said. "But before we even get there, we need to make sure that these data centers are not harming the local infrastructure, like the water and electricity."

Debate turns to election rules and 2020 denialism

Multiple times during the debate Collins was asked whether Trump prevailed in the 2020 election over former President Joe Biden.

He never answered yes or no, but instead said Biden "went into office," before adding "and boy, Georgians paid for it." Collins has falsely asserted Trump won Georgia six years ago during this campaign, including shortly before the Republican primary race.

Later, Collins expressed support for the administration's call to overhaul U.S. elections under the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, or SAVE America Act, which stalled in the Senate this year.

The measure would have, among other things, required registered voters to present a form of approved photo identification such as a passport or driver's license before receiving a ballot.

"You know the problem is that we have voter ID here in Georgia. We do, but when offered the opportunity at least five times, Jon Ossoff voted against the SAVE Act to get voter ID for all across this country," Collins said.

"Y'all, we live in the best country in the world. There's no reason we shouldn't have the most secure elections in the world."

Ossoff responded by slamming his opponent for supporting the establishment of a fund for participants in the Jan. 6, 2021 riot at the U.S. Capitol. In August, a video showed Collins agreeing with a Georgia man who was convicted of charges stemming from the attack and who suggested that the rioters were "victims of a weaponized political system."

"Mike Collins is on record supporting handing your tax dollars to the violent thugs and criminals who sacked the U.S. Capitol and tried to overturn the election," Ossoff said.

news.title: Iran War and heating oil take center stage in Maine Senate debate
news.text:
President Donald Trump, the Iran war and home heating oil took center stage in the third debate between five-term Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and former state Senate President Troy Jackson, a Democrat, in the race for U.S. Senate.

The race has garnered national attention as Democrats see the seat as key to their hopes of flipping the U.S. Senate, which is currently held by Republicans 53-47. The seat is rated a “toss-up” by the Cook Political Report and other forecasters.

The debate was hosted by WABI and WGAM, stations that service the more central and northern, rural and conservative parts of the state – a key constituency for candidates to win over. Both Collins and Jackson are from Aroostook County, which is the northernmost part of the state bordering Canada.

The candidates will face off one more time on Oct. 15. Here are three takeaways from the debate on Oct. 13.

Home heating oil is a major issue in Maine

Home heating oil has emerged as a major issue in Maine. According to the state, 52% of Maine households rely on heating oil to get them through the long winters. An average of 20 residents die every year from hypothermia, and carbon monoxide poisoning, sometimes caused by turning to alternative burning devices, is responsible for 70 emergency visits each year, according to data from 2024.

The cost of heating oil in Maine has jumped about 80% from last year, driven in part by the war in Iran.

Collins and Jackson clashed over who is more responsible for the high price of heating oil: Collins blamed Jackson and state leadership in general, while Jackson blamed the war in Iran.

Collins also heaped blame onto the Biden administration for cancelling projects like the Keystone Pipeline that she said would have expanded their supply of energy. Jackson said that the pipeline would have helped the U.S. ship oil overseas, not to Mainers.

Collins highlighted what she has done to help, including getting an earlier release of Low-Income Heating Assistance Program (LIHEAP) assistance. Jackson called it a “short-term Band-Aid.”

The Iran war continued to dominate part of the discussion, with the candidates quibbling over how much Collins did or didn’t support it. Collins initially supported the war but has opposed it for months.

Collins said that she doesn’t think Trump had a good plan and should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which is where a chunk of the world’s oil trade passes through. She said it’s important to make sure that Iran can’t make a nuclear weapon. She also said American troops need to be protected.

“My ideal end of this war would be an agreement by Iran that it would stop pursuing the enrichment of uranium for a nuclear weapon and the pursuit of long-range ballistic missiles,” Collins said.

Jackson argued that Collins could have stopped Trump from starting the war, then she opposed it when it was too late. Collins stressed that she has joined Democrats in voting against the war several times, but that they didn’t have the votes.

“Well, that sounds like then we probably ought to have Democrats in charge of the U.S. Senate so that we have the votes to stop this war,” Jackson replied.

Has Collins done enough?

Throughout the night, Collins highlighted specific policy achievements that she’s made during her time in the Senate. And repeatedly, Jackson responded that her efforts weren't enough.

Collins said she lifted tariffs on key items like concrete, road salt and pulp, but Jackson said Collins should have prevented the tariffs from being imposed in the first place.

Collins pointed out the $50 billion-dollar rural healthcare fund she successfully added to the One Big Beautiful Bill, but Jackson said that it won’t be enough to offset the negative healthcare impacts of the bill. Collins said she proposed and enacted reforms for ICE like body-worn cameras, but Jackson said that ICE should be disbanded.

Collins discussed a bipartisan housing bill she helped to pass that prevents private equity from buying up single-family homes, but Jackson rebutted that it doesn’t include apartment buildings, condos or mobile home parks.

Both arguments encapsulate the two candidates’ central platforms: Collins maintains she has the experience and knowledge needed to get things done for Maine, and Jackson argues that Collins has not done enough to stop the harm he thinks Trump has brought to Maine. 

“Our Constitution guarantees that regardless of population, each state has two senators, but it does not guarantee that all 100 senators will have the same knowledge, experience, and clout,” Collins said in her closing statement. “When you live in a small state like Maine, who you send to Washington really matters. I have proven time and time again that I deliver for the state of Maine.”

Jackson leaned into the oft-cited argument against Collins: that despite stressing her moderation, she doesn’t stand up to Trump enough.

“Senator Collins wants credit for her power. I believe you have to be responsible for what you do with it,” Jackson said. “Senator Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger. That's the choice on this stage: a senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine, then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price.”

 JC booted from Walker Cup for fielding ineligible player Jamone Lyle 

True Blues banned from 2027 knockout competition, must forfeit Manning Cup match against St Catherine 






Jamaica College (JC) have been booted from the Walker Cup for fielding an ineligible player, bringing their championship hopes crashing down just days before a highly anticipated final showdown against rivals Kingston College (KC).

Additionally, the ‘True Blues’ have been banned from next year’s edition of the knockout tournament, and must forfeit the Manning Cup second round match against St Catherine which they had won 3 – 2, which means the result has been reversed to hand St Catherine a 3 – 0 win over the many-time champions.

The decision was made at an ISSA emergency meeting on Tuesday, following the revelation that JC star Jamone Lyle has a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) regulations.

Waterhouse, in a disciplinary letter dated October 9, said it had fined Lyle $60,000 for unauthorised participation in a Manning Cup match on October 7. The club alleged that Lyle ignored instructions from head coach Donovan Duckie and General Secretary Richard McCallum not to take the field for JC, in breach of his professional contract and the club’s rules.

ISSA’s decision to boot JC from the Walker Cup means that KC will now face Mona High in the final set for Friday. Mona had lost to JC in the semi-final via a penalty shootout.

news.title: Vance announces Defense Production Act expansion of Texas refinery
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 14 (IANS) US Vice President JD Vance said the Trump administration had used the Defense Production Act to expand an oil refinery in Tyler, Texas, as he campaigned for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton three weeks before the midterm elections. "Today, I am pleased to announce that the Trump administration working with the refinery at Delek has used the Defense Production Act, and we are going to expand the refinery right here in Tyler, Texas," Vance told the rally. "We want millions of gallons of commercial grade and military spec fuel to come out of this refinery in addition to what it's already producing," he said. He said the expansion would "mean hundreds of good paying new jobs" in Smith County and lower fuel and travel costs for families. He did not give a cost or the planned increase in capacity. The Tyler refinery, owned by Delek US Holdings, processes about 74,000 barrels a day. The administration has used the Cold War-era law to back energy projects as high fuel prices weigh on household budgets ahead of the November 3 elections. In April, President Donald Trump signed a determination under the Act declaring domestic petroleum production, refining and logistics capacity essential to national defence. Vance turned the announcement into a pitch for Paxton, the Texas Attorney General, who is running for the US Senate against Democrat James Talarico. "He fights for you every single day and number two, he delivers he's not just a talker he's a guy who gets things done," Vance said of Paxton. Vance accused Talarico of "contempt" for the oil and gas industry. "Talarico says Texas energy dominance is like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s," Vance said. "He says jobs like the ones at the Texas refinery in Tyler aren't going to last." "If we elect Ken Paxton and we continue to support an energy dominance agenda ladies and gentlemen, Texas oil and gas jobs are going to be safe, and we're going to build more of them," he said. "We will never abandon the men and women of the oil and gas industry of Texas," Vance said. Vance also said Talarico had backed rejecting a ten-year minimum sentence for human smugglers and wanted the southern border to have "a giant welcome mat for the drug cartels". "That's what's on the ballot, ladies and gentlemen, on November 3rd," Vance said. "This November, let's send Ken Paxton to Washington and let's get back to work for the United States of America." Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, a Texan, attended the rally. Vance also briefly called out a protester waving a Mexican flag near the stage, saying, "we'll kick her out". Energy prices have been a central issue in the midterm campaign.

news.title: Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US  - Puerto Rico Tribune – Daily Puerto
news.text:
The Caribbean country of Jamaica has received its first third-country deportations from the United States, as part of an expanding set of international agreements under President Donald Trump.

On Tuesday, 22 deportees from the US arrived at Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston, Jamaica.

Media reports indicate they were subsequently boarded onto a bus and taken to an undisclosed location.

Such deportations – which often involve non-citizens who have no ties to their destinations – have faced widespread condemnation from human rights groups and advocates who have questioned their legality.

But Jamaica is among a growing number of countries to accept third-country deportations, as part of Trump’s effort to implement the largest mass deportation campaign in US history.

At least 35 countries have entered into third-country deportation agreements with the US, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, an advocacy project affiliated with the groups Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The Washington Post reported last month that the Trump administration has earmarked roughly $410m to support such efforts.

Jamaica signed a bilateral memorandum of understanding in June to receive third-country deportations. Under the plan, Jamaica will transfer any deportees to their home countries or other destinations after their arrival.

The country’s government has also pledged not to accept any deportees with criminal records.

“The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries,” Jamaica’s Ministry of National Security and Peace and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade said in a joint statement.

It added that care for the deportees will be supported by the International Organization for Migration, a United Nations organisation.

“The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica,” the joint statement added.

Opposition leaders in Jamaica, however, spoke out against the deportation, framing the deal as a threat to the island’s security. They also questioned why the agreement had not been debated publicly.

“Jamaicans are being asked to trust a secret document that touches their security, their communities and their public services,” said Fitz Jackson, the opposition spokesperson on national security.

In response to Jackson’s statement, Foreign Minister Kamina Johnson Smith argued that any questions about the deportation deal “have all been answered”. She also indicated that the US has not agreed to make the deal public.

“As I explained before, some countries have agreed to receive criminals, we have not,” she wrote on social media.

“Some countries have had their agreements made public, but our partner has not agreed for this one to be.”

Legal challenges against the third-country deportations are ongoing in the US, where advocates have argued that deportees are being removed from the country without due process of law, the constitutional right to a fair hearing.

Critics have also argued that third-country deportations sometimes send immigrants to countries where they may face danger.

Some of the recipient countries, such as South Sudan, are in the midst of ongoing conflict or have faced accusations of serious human rights abuses.

Opponents have even said the third-country deportations are being used as a backdoor method for circumventing court protection orders.

Such orders may prohibit the US government from returning certain immigrants to their home countries, for fear of violence and persecution.

But by sending immigrants to third countries, critics say the Trump administration avoids violating such protection orders – though in some cases, the third country has then returned the deportee to the country identified in the US protection order.

In a February report by Democrats on the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, one official said anonymously that the purpose of such far-flung deportations was to instil fear.

“The point is that the administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere,” the official said. “The point is to scare people.”

news.title: Rubio to Visit India Oct 17-22 to Boost Strategic and Energy Cooperation
news.text: Washington: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to India next week to further strengthen energy cooperation, the Department of State said on Tuesday. Rubio will first visit Samarkand in Uzbekistan, and will then travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar in India from October 17-22, it said.This will be Rubio's second visit to India since May, when he attended the Quad Foreign Ministers' meeting hosted by External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in New Delhi."He will meet with senior government officials to strengthen the US-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation," the State Department said.Rubio will also meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation, it said.Rubio's visit to Jamnagar is crucial as it is home to Reliance's refinery, the world's largest single-site facility with a capacity to process 1.4 million barrels per day of crude oil.In March, President Donald Trump announced that the US will build its first refinery in 50 years with investment from Reliance Industries.The refinery will come up at Brownsville in Texas at a cost of USD 300 billion, Trump said.In Samarkand, Rubio will participate in the C5+1 Ministerial to highlight how strategic cooperation through this diplomatic platform promotes a more peaceful and prosperous future for the United States and the countries of Central Asia.The Secretary will also participate in bilateral engagements with senior officials from all C5 countries -- Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Kyrgyz Republic.A US commercial delegation comprising over 200 business leaders will accompany Rubio, ushering in a new era of strengthened commercial cooperation for the United States and Central Asia.

news.title: Zelensky defies Trump's warnings with Ukraine drone strike on Russian oil depot
news.text: Ukraine has allegedly hit an oil facility in Russia despite cautions from US President Donald Trump . Over 500 drones are thought to have been deployed against Vladimir Putin's Russia during the night and video clips revealed the consequences of what seemed to be a catastrophic assault. The offensive represents the first Ukrainian attack on energy infrastructure since Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" mere days before. Earlier this week, Trump maintained that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to cease targeting each other's energy infrastructure. The US also warned it would sever intelligence sharing and suspend the PURL weapons system if Kyiv resumed energy attacks. Kyiv replied with: "We will burn Russian refineries." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated Russian forces had targeted at least six Ukrainian energy installations since the US president announced the truce on Sunday. Energy infrastructure has been a recurring target for both nations. Ukraine has progressively focused on Russian oil refineries and supply chains with long-range assaults in retaliation to Russian bombardments since the conflict began more than four-and-a-half years ago. Russia has continuously attempted to disable Ukraine's electricity and heating during successive winters. On Tuesday, the UK's foreign affairs ministry confirmed Zelensky would reach the UK during the morning and Britain urged international allies to intensify sanctions on Russia and increase pressure on Putin to honour the US appeals for an energy ceasefire. Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated, prior to his meeting with Zelensky, "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. :My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. "It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do. Russia's aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."
news.summary: Ukraine has reportedly carried out a drone strike on a Russian oil depot despite warnings from US President Donald Trump over the energy ceasefire

news.title: Ice cold: Even in Alaska, Trump can’t avoid being protested at rally — breaks out more ‘your mom’ shots
news.text:
President Donald Trump can’t avoid being protested at his rallies as he campaigns for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections — including in red-leaning Alaska. 

Amid record-low approval ratings, Trump is attempting to fire up his base to vote for members of his party as if he were on the ballot, as he often tells them to do. But the president has faced resistance from a series of lone protesters who have interrupted his rallies in Texas, Ohio and now Alaska. 

What is Trump’s savvy retort? “Your mom” jokes. 

Shortly after Trump took the stage in Wasilla, Alaska, at around 8:30 p.m. ET on Tuesday, a protester turned heads. 

As the president was bashing his 2024 presidential opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, he stopped to call the demonstrator a “spoiled child.”

“Sounds like we have a spoiled child,” Trump said as his supporters booed at the protester and chanted “USA, USA, USA.” 

As the protester, wearing a sweatshirt with a picture of a bald eagle carrying an American flag on it, was being escorted out, the president commended the “good law enforcement.” 

“He’s now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father, who both voted for me, by the way,” Trump said of the protester. 

Alaskans have voted for the Republican presidential nominee since at least 1980, according to 270toWin. Trump won the vote with 51.3 percent support in 2016, 52.8 percent in 2020 and 54.5 percent in 2024. 

Trump was in Youngstown, Ohio, last night, stumping for Sen. Jon Husted, who is running against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, and Vivek Ramaswamy, who ran against Trump for president in 2024 before endorsing him. Ramaswamy is running for governor in Ohio against Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health. 

During last night’s rally, Trump gushed about how attractive and athletic Husted, a college football star, was, telling a crowd of his supporters, “I looked at his a**, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these like claws.”

During one of two protests last night, Trump said the demonstrators “get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum.”

He then taunted the demonstrator currently causing a commotion, saying, “He's going back home to mom...He's got to go on a diet. He's a fat guy.”

“What he doesn't know is that his mother and father voted for me,” the president added, using a similar insult that he used against a protester in San Antonio, Texas, last week. 

Wasilla was Trump’s latest stop as he vigorously campaigns in red states with the midterms right around the corner. The president is trying to boost Republican candidates’ chances as he struggles with his own image issues. 

A whopping 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s job as president, while just 32 percent approved in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The Trump administration has been dogged by an unpopular war in Iran and stubborn inflation affecting Americans at the gas pump and grocery store. 

While the party in power typically loses seats in the midterm elections, recent polling shows Democrats gaining ground in Senate races in states that Republicans would normally coast through.

Mary Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman, is beating Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 7 percentage points, 50 to 43 percent, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters in Alaska released earlier this month. 

Peltola led by a slimmer margin in a poll recently released by Alaska Survey Research. The Democrat was just two percentage points ahead of Sullivan, 47 to 45 percent, among Alaska’s likely voters.
news.summary: Trump fumed at a protester in Wasilla, Alaska, calling them a ‘spoiled child,’ among other insults, after they interrupted his stump speech for Republican Senate candidate Dan Sullivan
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Donald Trump launches attack on 'spoiled child' as protester disrupts Alaska rally
news.text: Donald Trump has launched another attack at an audience member after his rally in Alaska was interrupted by a heckler. The US President has travelled to Alaska ahead of the crucial midterm elections, in the hope of drumming up more support before election day on November 3. But, all did not go as planned as he was speaking about his 2024 victory against former Vice President Kamala Harris , with an altercation taking place in the crowd, The US Mirror reports . "Sounds like we have a spoiled child," Trump said as the audience booed. The camera quickly panned over to the situation, but quickly returned to Trump, who praised the police. "Wow, good law enforcement!" he said. As he was escorted out, Trump added: “He’s now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father who both voted for me, by the way.” It comes after a similar incident a day earlier in Youngstown, where a female heckler was punched in the face by a male attendee before security stepped in to remove her from the event. During the incident, Trump referred to the woman as a "fat guy" who needs to "go on a diet." Nearly an hour behind schedule, the president took the stage just after 4:20 p.m. local time in Wasilla. The rally is being held at a local hockey arena. On the rink, there are seats where the ice would otherwise be. Many in the crowd were seen waving American flags and “Make America Great Again” caps. The events were planned to boost support for Alaskan Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is in a heated race that could determine whether Republicans keep control of the Senate after the midterms next month. Sullivan faces a challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who received more votes than Sullivan did in Alaska's open primary in August. During his speech, the US President announced what he claimed was “one of the biggest deals ever made”, claiming that Taiwan will purchase gas from a natural gas project in Alaska that Senator Dan Sullivan is touting in his reelection campaign. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. There were also no immediate further details from the White House. “Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years,” Trump said. “That guarantees success. It’s one of the biggest commitments in history for anything. It’s one of the biggest deals ever made.” Taiwan has also agreed to invest more than $4 billion in the project, Trump said. The president had similarly touted a $54 billion investment from South Korea in the Alaska pipeline, although South Korean officials had initially said the country needed to assess the project’s viability before actually committing to it.
news.summary: It comes just one day after another protester at a rally by the US President was punched in the face by a male attendee before security stepped in to remove her from the event

news.title: Trump debates calling off livestream of firing squad execution after learning Fort Hood shooter was paralyzed
news.text: President Donald Trump and his advisers are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter, with Trump having remarked privately that he did not initially know that Nidal Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down, two sources familiar with the discussions told CNN.The president was not aware that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was announcing last week that the administration planned to let the public watch the execution, the sources said, and was not sure what to make of it at first. Trump was, however, firmly behind the decision to execute Hasan via firing squad, multiple officials told CNN, and he’s often defended it in public.And even after Hegseth posted on X on Thursday confirming that the Pentagon planned to livestream the execution, Trump polled several of his advisers and allies about how to proceed.It was during the those conversations that Trump learned Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down — he was shot in the back by law enforcement during the 2009 shooting at Ford Hood — and that he now uses a wheelchair, the sources said, which made showing the execution publicly less palatable to the president.One of the sources familiar with the discussions pointed to Trump’s deep understanding of imagery as a key reason why he may decide to ditch plans for the livestream. The president has also listened to the argument that a public execution by firing squad could serve as propaganda for foreign adversaries and terrorists to try to paint Hasan as a martyr, a Trump adviser told CNN.The White House on Tuesday referred CNN to the president’s comments on Saturday in which he acknowledged “two thoughts” about what to do and said he’d make the ultimate decision.“He was vicious. He was violent,” Trump told reporters about Hasan over the weekend. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So, I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”RELATED STORY | Experts urge parents to prepare kids for possible livestreamed executionThe Pentagon is also reevaluating plans to fully livestream the execution, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Even if there is a broadcast of the event, the source said, it will likely be cut before shots are fired, in part, due to concerns that the moment could offer a propaganda opportunity for terrorist groups.Hegseth’s office has not responded to additional requests for comment about whether plans to livestream the execution have changed.The plan to livestream the execution has faced bipartisan backlash, and people across the Pentagon and the Army were caught off guard, CNN has previously reported.Trump told reporters on Friday that he was not involved but said, “I understand the decision,” adding that some people “want to set an example” by livestreaming the execution.Hegseth had initially recommended death by firing squad for Hasan — who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding dozens of others — and Trump approved it.The execution, which is scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the US Army’s first such execution of a soldier since World War II and its first imposition of any death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years.A US-born citizen of Palestinian descent, Hasan said he was targeting soldiers he was set to deploy with to Afghanistan and wanted to protect the Taliban and its leaders from the US military.The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. news.summary: President Trump and advisers are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter, with Trump noting that he did not know that Nidal Hasan was paralyzed.
news.author: Alayna Treene

news.title: Human rights groups criticize uncontested election of 15 countries to top UN human rights body
news.text:
Human rights groups sharply criticized Tuesday's uncontested election of 15 members of the United Nations’ premier human rights body, saying it resulted in countries with poor rights records winning seats.

Positions on the 47-nation Human Rights Council are allocated to the U.N.’s regional groups to ensure geographical representation. And for the second year in a row, all regional groups put forward the exact number of candidates for available seats for the three-year term. This meant that in Tuesday’s election in the 193-member General Assembly there were no competitive races.

“This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election,’” said Louis Charbonneau, U.N. director at Human Rights Watch. “No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter.”

He called on U.N. member nations to “insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records.”

In Tuesday’s vote, the Africa group’s Zambia, Ghana, Nigeria and Burundi were elected. The Asia-Pacific group’s Kuwait, Nepal, Jordan and Japan won seats. So did the Latin America and Caribbean group’s Brazil, Dominican Republic and Uruguay. The mainly Western group’s Ireland and Germany and the Central and East European group’s Moldova and Ukraine will also join the Human Rights Council.

The Geneva-based council reviews the human rights records of all countries periodically, appoints independent investigators to report on issues such as torture and situations in countries such as North Korea, Iran and Myanmar, and sends fact-finding missions to investigate rights violations. These include in Ukraine, the Palestinian territories and Israel and Sudan — all currently engulfed in conflict.

The council was created in 2006 to replace a human rights commission that was discredited because of some members’ poor rights records. But the new council soon came to face similar criticism, including that countries sought seats to protect themselves and their allies.

Soon after starting his second term, President Donald Trump announced the withdrawal of the United States from the Human Rights Council, He also pulled the U.S. out in his first term. accusing it of anti-Israel bias.

In its criticism of Tuesday's vote, Human Rights Watch singled out the “abusive human rights conditions” in the central African nation of Burundi. It said that despite some positive government statements, “Burundi has not carried out meaningful reform to address longstanding concerns related to governance, justice or accountability.”

It also said Nigeria should ensure accountability for serious crimes committed during the conflict with the armed group Boko Haram by all parties, including security forces. Brazil needs to “investigate and curb police abuse” after last year’s killing of more than 6,500 people — the vast majority of them Black — by law enforcement officers, it said.

While Ukraine has suffered “countless atrocities committed by Russian forces,” Human Rights Watch said Ukrainian authorities have also “unjustly prosecuted Ukrainian civilians living under Russian occupation” for doing permitted work, including as teachers, medics, municipal workers and volunteers.

The International Service for Human Rights, a Geneva=based organization that supports rights defenders, said never has the work of the council been so essential. 

“States with a real commitment to upholding human rights should be doing everything they can to ensure the body includes states that uphold the highest human rights standards," said Madeleine Sinclair, director of its New York office. 

U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric, responding to a question about the U.N. position on the uncontested vote, said it’s a matter for the 193 member nations. “But what we’ve always said is that member states who are elected to this organization’s highest human rights body have an added responsibility to protect human rights, not only in their own home country, but also to be strong advocates for human rights globally,” he said.
news.summary: Human rights groups are sharply criticizing the uncontested election of 15 members of the United Nations' premier human rights body, saying it resulted in countries with poor rights records winning seats
news.author: Edith M. Lederer
